title: The Multiplicity Factor Theorem in All Characteristics via Hasse Derivatives
description: The parent (factor-remainder-theorem-oq-01) proves the multiplicity factor theorem (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p ↔ p, p′, …, p^{(k−1)} vanish at a, but only over a characteristic-zero field — its proof divides by the factorials produced by ordinary iterated derivatives. In positive characteristic that fails: over ZMod p the polynomial Xᵖ has every ordinary derivative identically zero. This entry proves the correct characteristic-free statement using Hasse (divided-power) derivatives: (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p ↔ ∀ m < k, (hasseDeriv m p)(a) = 0, valid over an arbitrary commutative ring and with no p ≠ 0 hypothesis, answering the parent's open question on extending to positive characteristic. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext:
The Factor Theorem says a is a root of p iff (X − a) ∣ p; its multiplicity refinement says (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff a is a root of multiplicity at least k. Over a field of characteristic zero this is equivalent to the vanishing of p together with its first k − 1 ordinary derivatives at a — the statement that the Taylor expansion of p at a begins at order k. The characteristic-zero hypothesis is essential for the derivative formulation: in characteristic p the derivative of Xᵖ is zero, so ordinary derivatives can all vanish without the multiplicity being large, and the equivalence collapses.

The remedy, introduced by Helmut Hasse, is the divided-power (Hasse) derivative hasseDeriv m, whose value at a is exactly the order-m Taylor coefficient (taylor a p).coeff m, computed without dividing by m!. Because no factorial is inverted, the Hasse derivative remains informative in every characteristic. This entry answers the parent's open question by proving the multiplicity factor theorem in Hasse form over an arbitrary commutative ring: (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p ↔ ∀ m < k, (hasseDeriv m p)(a) = 0, with no characteristic and no nonvanishing hypothesis.
overview.problemStatement: Prove the multiplicity factor theorem in positive (indeed arbitrary) characteristic using Hasse derivatives: over any commutative ring R, for p ∈ R[X], a ∈ R and k ∈ ℕ, (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff (hasseDeriv m p)(a) = 0 for all m < k. Record the k = 1 (Factor Theorem) and k = 2 (double root) cases, the rootMultiplicity reading, and an explicit ZMod 2 witness showing ordinary derivatives fail where Hasse derivatives succeed.
overview.proofStrategy: The Taylor shift τ : q ↦ q.comp (X + C a) is a ring automorphism of R[X] carrying X − a to X, so (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p ↔ Xᵏ ∣ taylor a p (pow_X_sub_C_dvd_iff_taylor, proved directly with the composition lemmas mul_comp/pow_comp/sub_comp/comp_assoc — no characteristic needed). Then Xᵏ ∣ q ↔ ∀ d < k, q.coeff d = 0 (X_pow_dvd_iff), and the d-th coefficient of taylor a p is precisely (hasseDeriv d p)(a) (taylor_coeff). Chaining these gives the Hasse multiplicity factor theorem in three rewrites. The k = 1 and k = 2 cases instantiate it and use hasseDeriv_zero'/hasseDeriv_one'. The rootMultiplicity reading rewrites le_rootMultiplicity_iff through the main theorem. The ZMod 2 witness computes (hasseDeriv 2 (X²))(0) = (taylor 0 (X²)).coeff 2 = (X²).coeff 2 = 1 while derivative (X²) = C 2 · X = 0 since 2 = 0 in ZMod 2.
keyInsights: The Hasse derivative is exactly the Taylor coefficient: (hasseDeriv m p)(a) = (taylor a p).coeff m, with no division by m!. This is why it works in every characteristic, where p^{(m)}(a)/m! is meaningless once m! = 0.

Multiplicity is the order of vanishing of the Taylor expansion. Transferring through the ring automorphism X ↦ X + a turns '(X − a)ᵏ ∣ p' into 'Xᵏ ∣ taylor a p', i.e. the first k Taylor coefficients vanish.

The divisibility characterization needs NO p ≠ 0 hypothesis (unlike rootMultiplicity, which is only defined relative to a nonzero polynomial), and NO characteristic hypothesis — a genuine strengthening of the parent.

In characteristic p ordinary derivatives are blind: over ZMod 2, derivative(X²) = 0, so the char-0 criterion would falsely certify (X)³ ∣ X²; the second Hasse derivative evaluates to 1, correctly refuting it.
The whole proof reduces to the substitution algebra (composition lemmas) plus two Mathlib facts (X_pow_dvd_iff, taylor_coeff) — a clean, reusable route to the multiplicity criterion.
prerequisites: Characteristic of a ring and vanishing factorials

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 131 lines and 6 theorems proving the multiplicity factor theorem in Hasse form over an arbitrary commutative ring: (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p ↔ ∀ m < k, (hasseDeriv m p)(a) = 0, with no characteristic and no p ≠ 0 hypothesis. It transfers divisibility through the Taylor shift X ↦ X + a, then reads off coefficient vanishing via X_pow_dvd_iff and taylor_coeff. The k = 1, k = 2, and rootMultiplicity cases follow, and an explicit ZMod 2 witness shows ordinary derivatives are blind where Hasse derivatives succeed.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent's open question on extending the multiplicity factor theorem to positive characteristic, and in fact gives a uniform statement valid in every characteristic and over any commutative ring. The Hasse form is the correct tool for detecting repeated roots in characteristic p (e.g. recognizing inseparability and the failure of squarefreeness tests based on gcd(p, p′)). The characterization is also cleaner than the char-0 version: it drops both the field and the p ≠ 0 hypotheses.
openQuestions: Relate this to separability: a polynomial over a field is separable iff it shares no root with its first Hasse derivative, and characterize inseparable irreducibles (those that are polynomials in Xᵖ) via the vanishing of all Hasse derivatives up to order p − 1.
Formalize the full Taylor expansion identity p = ∑ₘ (hasseDeriv m p)(a) · (X − a)ᵐ over an arbitrary commutative ring, of which the multiplicity factor theorem is the order-of-vanishing reading.
